title: Tribal rhythm and jazz; Ted Lewis and Victor Young in Chicago theaters
summary: Asked about similarity between tribal and jazz rhythm, Moore recalls hanging around Chicago theaters hearing Ted Lewis and Victor Young.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: When I said at the beginning of this tape that I think everybody---every human being from days a long time ago---always had some kind of a rhythm and blues....(Pause) And when I think of the years that I spent in Chicago it was really the start of my induction into jazz music, besides the other facets of classical concert work that I did. The background was there and the way that I learned to project listening to all those other bands---at one time when I was in a theater on the North Side of Chicago, Ted Lewis was there. And I remember George Brunies was in that band. This was in 192-----that was the year I was

there in Chicago, in 1929. They were playing "She's Funny That Way", you know -- "I'm not much to look at, nothing to see; just good on living and lucky to be" -- that tune. And then they played "Wear a Hat With a Silver Lining". And that was beautiful; I loved that. And during the stage shows I'd be inside, and then during the picture I'd be out and waiting for the next stage show, and I just hung around there all day. Didn't have nothin' to do but listen to music. And that was one of the experiences that I had with Ted Lewis.

I didn't get to see Goldkett, but I've heard him on the radio, and then I -- that was at the Oriental Theater was a fellow by the name of Victor Young who later went to, went on to Hollywood to, to be an orchestra leader there. And he was at the Oriental Theater then, and I used to go hear him all the time.
